content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors show that the CLIP model has a task bias where the visual representation learned will prefer to solve one task over another task. The tasks here include object recognition, action recognition, and scene text recognition. The common method of using different task-specific text prompts does not work well because although the text feature is changed, the visual feature is fixed no matter what the text prompt is. Thus, the authors propose to use task-specific visual prompts so that the visual prompt can control the generation of the visual feature so that it can bias toward the task being tackled. To evaluate and train such visual prompts, the authors build up a benchmark dataset. The authors show that the proposed visual prompt-based methods are better than text prompts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The proposed method does not require the retraining of the whole model.
- The authors justify their method by showing that text prompting is not enough to fix this issue and also show that task bias is often unintuitive to humans.
- The authors provide visualization to show how the task-specific visual prompts can guide the attentions in the transformer.

Weaknesses:
- I personally have a hard time being motivated by the authors’ example in figure 1. The main reason is that it is clear to me that VLMs are biased towards some tasks because they are pre-trained on some pretext tasks. In CLIP, it is the image caption retrieval task. So which text best describes the image or which text can mostly discriminate the described image from other images should have the highest score given CLIP. The figure 1 result makes perfect sense to me and I really didn’t think that is a problem when I read the introduction. To me, they may be equally correct, but not equally good.
- Another limitation of this paper is the authors are focusing on the CLIP model which is a two-tower model. Because of that, the text prompt won’t work so well because it can only modulate the text part but not the visual part. However, there are also many single-stream VLMs which may not have the same problem because the text prompt will be able to affect how visual information is attended. I think it would be interesting to see how the conclusion in this paper can transfer to other VLMs.
- The authors show that by learning the visual prompts the authors can select the “correct” task output from all “correct” answers. However, the authors didn’t do much downstream experiments when including incorrect answers. The only result is in table 2, the OpenImageClassification. As shown in table 2, it seems that it is possible that the proposed method would make the visual feature lose the ability to tell the correct answer from incorrect answers. (VITP is getting higher  scores in Table 1 but lower in table2). More experiments on text and scene classification are wanted.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Minor: 
- page 6 f\phi mismatches Eq1 g\phi.

Questions:
- The use case I can think of it is it allows kind of few-shot learning or low sample size learning, where you have a small number of samples that you can use to learn a prompt, then use the learned prompt to do the task. So, first, how many samples are needed to learn such a prompt? Second, how is the generalizability? Say if I train on a dataset with only dog recognition subset of imagenet, would it transfer to other categories in imagenet?
- Section 3.3 is a critical baseline, but it is not clear how it is done. When the authors say performance increases on one task, what does that mean? In addition, from the text, the authors show that when comparing text task to other tasks, using the text-specific prompt will increase the performance. Why do the authors say text prompt is not consistent?

Novelty: the technique is not entirely novel, but the finding of the problem and the dataset may be novel to the community.
Reproducibility: the method can likely be reproduced given the information provided in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Althought the authors present the task bias problem of the CLIP model, my biggest complaint is that the authors do not show how their method can benefit other tasks that use pre-trained CLIP and may suffer from the CLIP task bias issue. Thus I decide to vote for borderline reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper empirically shows that the pretrained CLIP model has task bias where the predictions are biased towards some other tasks that are not intended. To tackle this issue, they propose to learn visual prompts as a condition for the target task. To evaluate the method, they construct a dataset and show some improvement.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

+ The first work to study representational task bias in visual-language model (VLM)
+ A simple approach that tackles the task ambiguity

Weakness

- Although the study is original, I am not convinced that the task ambiguity/bias issue is so important. The observations seem to be expected because the model is pretrained in an unsupervised manner where the downstream task is unknown. Once the model is fine-tuned for a downstream task, I would expect the task bias will be gone.  Therefore, this observation is only valid for zero-shot applications where we assume that no labeled training example is available. 

-If the representation is bias towards some tasks that are unintended, why not simply remove those options at the label space? From performance point of view, this solution is totally fine for the downstream task

-It would be interesting to investigate why some tasks are preferred over some others. I think this is because of the training set is biased to those tasks.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper is written well and easy to follow

The paper is also the first work to study task bias issue in VLM. 

Quality: I find the quality a bit limited because the motivation of the problem is not convincing.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the study of task bias in VLM is new, I am afraid that the phenomenon is expected because the model is pretrained in an unsupervised manner and know nothing about the target task. The paper is filled with observations but fails to investigate why the bias is happening. In addition, I hope the authors can address my concerns about: 1) why not simply fine-tune the model on downstream task to alleviate the bias? 2) why not simply remove the tasks that are not relevant from the label space?

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Motivation: This paper suggests that for many images, there may be multiple correct labels, depending on the desired task. This poses a problem for Vision-Language models, such as CLIP which are pre-trained without knowledge of the downstream task. While there are multiple correct labels, different ones are preferred by CLIP for different images. 

Method: The authors of this work collect labels for 3 example tasks (object recognition, action recognition and OCR) for a set of images. They then learn features which can be added to image in order to steer the predictions of the model to the desired task. They do this in two ways (adding information to the images in pixel space and in latent space).

Results: The authors show that they are able to move the final embeddings of the image closer to the desired text embedding than to the text embedding associated with correct, but irrelevant, labels nearly 100% of the time. They show improved accuracy on OpenImages object recognition. They also show some qualitative results on downstream tasks by showing that the attention of the model changes depending on which task they are focusing on.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
-straightforward approach which increases in ability to predict correct task
-approach is well motivated and suited to problem


Weaknesses:
-no quantitative results on downstream tasks other than openImages, which is the dataset used for training. Train/test splits are used, but it is important to know if learned visual prompts really capture the notion of a "task" beyond this distribution.  I would be interested to see accuracy for the datasets used by Ilharco et al and Goh et al. instead of just qualitative results
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
While approach is well suited to the task, it is not novel. Authors have used an existing approach for a new application.

Some of the figures could be clearer in the following ways:
1. Included the "text prompt engineering" baseline in table 1 for easier comparison
2. Include the 2 relevant labels for the each image in figure 4
content.summary_of_the_review: While the technique is not novel, it is applied to an interesting and relevant problem. I would increase my score to accept if this was shown to increase accuracy on datasets beyond the dataset used for training.

content.title: Representational Task Bias in Zero-shot Recognition at Scale
content.TL;DR: We show CLIP image representations are biased towards being used for a specific task a priori, and provide a simple method cue which task is desired without model retraining.
content.abstract: Research from the last year has demonstrated that vision-language pre-training at scale from incidental supervision on the Internet can result in representations with clear advantages over traditional supervised training for many computer vision tasks. We conduct an in-depth exploration of the CLIP model, and find that the interface that language creates to these learned representations -- by the same token as enabling zero-shot application for many tasks -- leads the model to solve tasks that may not have been intended by the user in realistic scenarios. We call the inherent uncertainty of which task a user intends to solve in zero-shot recognition \textit{task ambiguity}. To evaluate task ambiguity, we construct a dataset of images where each image has labels for multiple semantic recognition tasks. We demonstrate that the representation produced for a given image tends to be strongly biased towards a particular task over others; in other words, they exhibit \textit{task bias}. Moreover, which task a particular image will be biased towards is unpredictable, with little consistency across images. Our results show that we can learn visual prompts to serve as effective conditioning mechanisms for which task is desired, and can even improve performance for the task when used outside the context of evaluating task ambiguity.
